It is situated in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Machupicchu_District" title="Machupicchu District" id="mwKA">Machupicchu District</a> of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Urubamba_Province" title="Urubamba Province" class="mw-redirect" id="mwKQ">Urubamba Province</a><sup about="#mwt70" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC20267_12-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC20267"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC20267-12"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"SERNANP"},"2":{"wt":"DCC"},"3":{"wt":"2026"},"p":{"wt":"7"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC20267-12" id="mwKg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwKw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwLA">[</span>10<span class="cite-bracket" href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstete2020a313-13" id="mwLg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwLw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMA">[</span>11<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwMQ">]</span></span></a></sup> about <span about="#mwt76" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"80"},"2":{"wt":"km"},"3":{"wt":"miles"},"sp":{"wt":"us"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwMg">80 kilometers (50 miles)</span> northwest of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cusco" title="Cusco" id="mwMw">Cusco</a>, above the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Sacred_Valley" title="Sacred Valley" id="mwNA">Sacred Valley</a> and along the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Urubamba_River" title="Urubamba River" id="mwNQ">Urubamba River</a>, which forms a deep canyon with a subtropical mountain climate.<sup about="#mwt77" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESpizzichinoMasiniLasaponaraMargottini202216–19_14-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESpizzichinoMasiniLasaponaraMargottini202216–19"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESpizzichinoMasiniLasaponaraMargottini202216–19-14"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Spizzichino"},"2":{"wt":"Masini"},"3":{"wt":"Lasaponara"},"4":{"wt":"Margottini"},"5":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"16–19"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpizzichinoMasiniLasaponaraMargottini202216–19-14" id="mwNg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwNw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOA">[</span>12<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwOQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwOg">Often referred to as the "Lost City of the Incas",<sup about="#mwt86" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-15" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-15"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-15" id="mwOw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwPA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPQ">[</span>13<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwPg">]</span></span></a></sup> Machu Picchu is one of the most iconic symbols of the Inca civilization and a major archaeological site in the Americas. Estimated to be built around 1450, it is believed to have served as an estate for the Inca emperor <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Pachacuti" title="Pachacuti" id="mwPw">Pachacuti</a>, though no contemporary written records exist to confirm this. The site was abandoned roughly a century later, likely during the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Spanish_conquest_of_Peru" title="Spanish conquest of Peru" class="mw-redirect" id="mwQA">Spanish conquest</a>. Modern <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Radiocarbon_dating#Accelerator_mass_spectrometry" title="Radiocarbon dating" id="mwQQ">radiocarbon dating</a> places its occupation between <abbr title="circa" about="#mwt80" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"circa","href":"./Template:Circa"},"params":{},"i":0}}]}' id="mwQg">c.</abbr> 1420 and 1530.<sup about="#mwt81" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273_16-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273-16"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"Nesbitt"},"4":{"wt":"Washburn"},"5":{"wt":"2021"},"p":{"wt":"1273"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273-16" id="mwQw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwRA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwRQ">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwRg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwRw">Machu Picchu was constructed in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_architecture" title="Inca architecture" id="mwSA">classical Inca style</a>, featuring finely crafted <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Dry-stone_wall" title="Dry-stone wall" class="mw-redirect" id="mwSQ">dry-stone walls</a>. Notable structures include the <i id="mwSg">Temple of the Sun</i>, the <i id="mwSw">Temple of the Three Windows</i>, and the <i id="mwTA"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Intihuatana,_Urubamba" title="Intihuatana, Urubamba" id="mwTQ">Intihuatana</a></i> ritual stone. Although the site was known locally and reached in the early 20th century by the Peruvian explorer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Agustín_Lizárraga" title="Agustín Lizárraga" id="mwTg">Agustín Lizárraga</a>, it was brought to international attention in 1911 by the American historian <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Hiram_Bingham_III" title="Hiram Bingham III" id="mwTw">Hiram Bingham III</a>. The original Inca name of the site may have been <i id="mwUA">Huayna Picchu</i>, after the mountain on which part of the complex stands.<sup about="#mwt87" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202226–27_17-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado GonzalesBauer202226–27"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202226–27-17"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amado Gonzales"},"2":{"wt":"Bauer"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"26–27"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202226–27-17" id="mwUQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwUg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwUw">[</span>15<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwVA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwVQ">Designated a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Historic_Sanctuary_of_Machu_Picchu" title="Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu" id="mwVg">National Historic Sanctuary</a> by Peru in 1981 and a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site" title="UNESCO World Heritage Site" class="mw-redirect" id="mwVw">UNESCO World Heritage Site</a> in 1983, Machu Picchu was also named one of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./New7Wonders_of_the_World#Winners" title="New7Wonders of the World" class="mw-redirect" id="mwWA">New Seven Wonders of the World</a> in 2007.<sup about="#mwt93" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-18" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-18"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-18" id="mwWQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwWg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwWw">[</span>16<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwXA">]</span></span></a></sup> <span about="#mwt90" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"As of","href":"./Template:As_of"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2025"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwXQ">As of 2025</span><sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;" about="#mwt90"><a rel="mw:ExtLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Machu_Picchu&amp;action=edit" class="external text" data-mw-original-href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Machu_Picchu&amp;action=edit"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span>update<span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></a></sup><span typeof="mw:Nowiki" about="#mwt90"></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements_from_2025" about="#mwt90"/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_containing_potentially_dated_statements" about="#mwt90" id="mwXg"/>, the site receives over 1.5 million visitors annually, making it Peru's most visited international tourist destination.</p>\n\n<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" data-mw='{"autoGenerated":true}' id="mwXw"/></section><section data-mw-section-id="1" id="mwYA"><h2 id="Etymology">Etymology</h2>\n<p id="mwYQ">The site is on a narrow saddle between two mountain peaks, Machu Picchu and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Huayna_Picchu" title="Huayna Picchu" id="mwYg">Huayna Picchu</a>. In the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Quechua_language" title="Quechua language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwYw">Quechua language</a>, <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt94" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[:wikt:machu#Quechua|machu]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwZA"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/machu#Quechua" title="wikt:machu" class="extiw">machu</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt94" id="mwZQ"/> means 'old' or 'old person' and <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt95" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[:wikt:wayna#Quechua|wayna]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwZg"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/wayna#Quechua" title="wikt:wayna" class="extiw">wayna</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt95" id="mwZw"/> (spelled <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt96" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"huayna"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwaA"><i lang="es">huayna</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt96" id="mwaQ"/> in standard <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Spanish_orthography" title="Spanish orthography" id="mwag">Spanish orthography</a>) means 'young', while <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt97" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[:wikt:pikchu#Quechua|pikchu]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwaw"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pikchu#Quechua" title="wikt:pikchu" class="extiw">pikchu</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt97" id="mwbA"/> refers to a 'summit', 'peak', or 'pyramid'.<sup about="#mwt98" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalvo_Pérez2022527,_739,_1271_19-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTECalvo Pérez2022527, 739, 1271"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTECalvo_Pérez2022527,_739,_1271-19"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Calvo Pérez"},"2":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"527, 739, 1271"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalvo_Pérez2022527,_739,_1271-19" id="mwbQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwbg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwbw">[</span>17<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwcA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt101" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-21" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"lower-alpha"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-21"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"efn","href":"./Template:Efn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"{{lang|qu|Pikchu}} may also refer to a \"portion of coca that is chewed\".{{sfn|Calvo Pérez|2022|p=739}}"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-21" data-mw-group="lower-alpha" id="mwcQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwcg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwcw">[</span>c<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwdA">]</span></span></a></sup> Thus, the name of the site is often translated as 'old mountain' or 'old peak'.<sup about="#mwt107" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELuciano201136_22-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTELuciano201136"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTELuciano201136-22"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Luciano"},"2":{"wt":"2011"},"p":{"wt":"36"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELuciano201136-22" id="mwdQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwdg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwdw">[</span>19<span class="cite-bracket" id="mweA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mweQ">Although the original name given to the settlement by its builders is not definitively known, a 2021 study in <i id="mweg"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ñawpa_Pacha" title="Ñawpa Pacha" id="mwew">Ñawpa Pacha</a>: Journal of the Institute of Andean Studies</i>  suggests that the site was likely called "Huayna Picchu", after the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Huayna_Picchu" title="Huayna Picchu" id="mwfA">smaller peak nearby</a>, or simply "Picchu". According to the research, the association of the name Machu Picchu with the ruins likely began with American explorer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Hiram_Bingham_III" title="Hiram Bingham III" id="mwfQ">Hiram Bingham</a>'s 1911 publications, a conclusion supported by Bingham's field notes, early maps, and historical documents.<sup about="#mwt110" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022_23-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado GonzalesBauer2022"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022-23"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amado Gonzales"},"2":{"wt":"Bauer"},"3":{"wt":"2022"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022-23" id="mwfg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwfw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwgA">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwgQ">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt115" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-24" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-24"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-24" id="mwgg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="History">History</h2>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwhw"><a href="./File:Machu_Picchu.png" class="mw-file-description" id="mwiA"><img loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Machu_Picchu.png/500px-Machu_Picchu.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" 1912 after major clearing and before reconstruction work began</figcaption></figure>\n\n<p id="mwjA">Machu Picchu’s early chronology continues to be a matter of scholarly debate. Earlier chronological models, based mainly on <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./John_H._Rowe" title="John H. Rowe" class="mw-redirect" id="mwjQ">John H. Rowe</a>'s <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Historical_reconstruction" title="Historical reconstruction" id="mwjg">historical reconstruction</a> of the reign of Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui, have placed the beginning of construction around 1450, 10 years after his takeover.<sup about="#mwt116" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERowe1945277_25-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion Burger</a>, professor of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Anthropology" title="Anthropology" id="mwnA">anthropology</a> at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Yale_University" title="Yale University" about="#mwt140" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEQuave2018109–110_31-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" Although Machu Picchu is considered to be a royal estate, it would not have been passed down in the line of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Order_of_succession" title="Order of succession" id="mwyg">succession</a>.<link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:All_articles_with_unsourced_statements" about="#mwt152" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Citation needed","href":"./Template:Citation_needed"},"params":{"date":{"wt":"August 2026"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwyw"/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_unsourced_statements_from_August_2026" about="#mwt152"/><sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;" about="#mwt152" id="mwzA"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span><i><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner2010516-37" id="mw6A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw6Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw6g">[</span>34<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw6w">]</span></span></a></sup> who lived there permanently. Though the estate belonged to Pachacutec, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Religion_in_the_Inca_Empire" title="Religion in the Inca Empire" id="mw7A">religious specialists</a> and temporary specialized workers (<span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt167" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"mayocs"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mw7Q"><i lang="qu">mayocs</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt167" id="mw7g"/>) lived there as well, most likely for the ruler's well-being and enjoyment. During winter, which was usually the harsher season, staffing was reduced to a few hundred servants, and a few religious specialists focused on maintenance alone.<sup about="#mwt168" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–87_38-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–87"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–87-38"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"pp":{"wt":"86–87"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–87-38" id="mw7w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw8A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw8Q">[</span>35<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw8g">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mw8w">Studies of skeletal remains found at Machu Picchu show that most people who lived there were immigrants from diverse backgrounds.<sup about="#mwt171" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8_39-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8-39"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salazar"},"2":{"wt":"Burger"},"3":{"wt":"Forst"},"4":{"wt":"Barquera"},"5":{"wt":"2023"},"pp":{"wt":"1–8"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8-39" id="mw9A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw9Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw9g">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw9w">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt174" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5_40-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5-40"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Turner"},"2":{"wt":"Armelagos"},"3":{"wt":"2012"},"pp":{"wt":"1–5"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5-40" id="mw-A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mw-Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mw-g">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket" id="mw-w">]</span></span></a></sup> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Genome-wide_association_study" title="Genome-wide association study" id="mw_A">Genome-wide</a> analyses indicate that the retainer community (<span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt177" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"yanacona"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mw_Q"><i lang="qu">yanacona</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt177" id="mw_g"/> and former <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt178" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[aclla]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mw_w"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Aclla" title="Aclla">aclla</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt178" id="mwAQA"/>) was genetically diverse, including Andean, coastal, Ecuadorian, and Amazonian ancestries, with individuals of different ancestries living, reproducing, and being buried together.<sup about="#mwt179" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8_39-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8-39"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salazar"},"2":{"wt":"Burger"},"3":{"wt":"Forst"},"4":{"wt":"Barquera"},"5":{"wt":"2023"},"pp":{"wt":"1–8"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazarBurgerForstBarquera20231–8-39" id="mwAQE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQM">[</span>36<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQQ">]</span></span></a></sup> They lacked the chemical markers and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Osteology" title="Osteology" id="mwAQU">osteological</a> markers they would have if they had been living there their entire lives. Instead, research into skeletal remains has found bone damage from various species of water <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Parasites_of_humans" title="Parasites of humans" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAQY">parasites</a> indigenous to different areas of Peru. There were also varying osteological stressors and varying chemical densities, suggesting varying long-term diets characteristic of specific regions that were spaced apart.<sup about="#mwt182" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5_40-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5-40"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Turner"},"2":{"wt":"Armelagos"},"3":{"wt":"2012"},"pp":{"wt":"1–5"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20121–5-40" id="mwAQc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAQg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQk">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAQo">]</span></span></a></sup> These diets are composed of varying levels of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Maize" title="Maize" id="mwAQs">maize</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Potato" title="Potato" id="mwAQw">potatoes</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Grain" title="Grain" id="mwAQ0">grains</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Legume" title="Legume" id="mwAQ4">legumes</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Fish" title="Fish" id="mwAQ8">fish</a>, but the last-known short-term diet for these people was overall composed of less fish and more corn. This suggests that several of the immigrants were from more coastal areas and moved to Machu Picchu, where corn was a larger portion of food intake.<sup about="#mwt185" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETurner2010526–529_41-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTETurner2010526–529"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner2010526–529-41"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Turner"},"2":{"wt":"2010"},"pp":{"wt":"526–529"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurner2010526–529-41" id="mwARA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwARE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARI">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARM">]</span></span></a></sup> Most skeletal remains found at the site had lower levels of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Arthritis" title="Arthritis" id="mwARQ">arthritis</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Bone_fracture" title="Bone fracture" id="mwARU">bone fractures</a> than those found in most sites of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_Empire" title="Inca Empire" id="mwARY">Inca Empire</a>. Incan individuals who had arthritis and bone fractures were typically those who performed heavy physical labor (such as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Mit'a" title="Mit'a" id="mwARc">Mit'a</a>) or served in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_army" title="Inca army" id="mwARg">Inca military</a>.<sup about="#mwt188" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200488_42-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200488"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200488-42"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"88"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200488-42" id="mwARk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwARo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARs">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwARw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAR0">Animals are also suspected to have been brought to Machu Picchu, as there were several bones found that were not native to the area. Most animal bones found were from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Llama" title="Llama" id="mwAR4">llamas</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Alpaca" title="Alpaca" id="mwAR8">alpacas</a>. These animals naturally live at altitudes of <span about="#mwt191" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"4000"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"-3"},"sp":{"wt":"us"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwASA">4,000 meters (13,000</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt191"> </span><span about="#mwt191">ft)</span> rather than the <span about="#mwt192" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2400"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"-2"},"sp":{"wt":"us"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwASE">2,400 meters (7,900</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt192"> </span><span about="#mwt192">ft)</span> elevation of Machu Picchu. Most likely, these animals were brought in from the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Puna_grassland" title="Puna grassland" id="mwASI">Puna</a> region for meat consumption and for their pelts.<sup about="#mwt193" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–94_43-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–94"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–94-43"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"pp":{"wt":"86–94"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200486–94-43" id="mwASM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASU">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt196" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller20038_44-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMiller20038"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller20038-44"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Miller"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"8"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller20038-44" id="mwASc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwASg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASk">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwASo">]</span></span></a></sup> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Guinea_pig" title="Guinea pig" id="mwASs">Guinea pigs</a> were also found at the site in special tomb caves, suggesting that they were at least used for funerary rituals,<sup about="#mwt199" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494_45-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494-45"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"94"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494-45" id="mwASw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAS0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAS4">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAS8">]</span></span></a></sup> as it was common throughout the Inca Empire to use them for sacrifices and meat.<sup about="#mwt202" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMalpass200938_46-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMalpass200938"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalpass200938-46"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Malpass"},"2":{"wt":"2009"},"p":{"wt":"38"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMalpass200938-46" id="mwATA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwATE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATI">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATM">]</span></span></a></sup> Six dogs were also recovered from the site. Due to their placements among the human remains, it is believed that they served as companions of the dead.<sup about="#mwt205" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494_45-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494-45"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"94"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200494-45" id="mwATQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwATU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATY">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwATc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="5" id="mwATg"><h4 id="Agricultural_activity">Agricultural activity</h4>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwATk"><a href="./File:Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_(cropped).jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwATo"><img resource="./File:Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_(cropped).jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_%28cropped%29.jpg/330px-Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_%28cropped%29.jpg/960px-Andenes_at_Machu_Picchu_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Stepped Inca agricultural terraces on a steep slope." data-file-width="3455" data-file-height="2236" data-file-type="bitmap" height="194" width="300" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.2" id="mwATs"/></a><figcaption id="mwATw">The <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt208" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"[[Andén|andenes]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAT0"><i lang="es"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Andén" title="Andén">andenes</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt208" id="mwAT4"/> (terraces) were mostly used for slope stabilization and corn cultivation.</figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwAT8">Much of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Incan_agriculture" title="Incan agriculture" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAUA">farming</a> carried out at Machu Picchu was done on its <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt209" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"[[Andén|andenes]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAUE"><i lang="es"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Andén" title="Andén">andenes</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt209" id="mwAUI"/> (artificial terraces). These terraces were a work of considerable engineering, built to ensure drainage and soil fertility while also protecting the mountain itself from erosion and landslides. However, the terraces were not perfect, as studies of the land show that there were landslides that happened during the construction of Machu Picchu. Still visible are places where the terraces were shifted by landslides and then stabilized by the Inca as they continued to build around the area.<sup about="#mwt210" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrown2001_47-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBrown2001"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Brown"},"2":{"wt":"2001"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47" id="mwAUM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAUQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUU">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUY">]</span></span></a></sup> The terraces also facilitated the management of water for agriculture, increasing crop yields, with maize likely being the main crop due to its ceremonial importance, alongside possible cultivation of potatoes.<sup about="#mwt213" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92_48-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92-48"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Reinhard"},"2":{"wt":"2007"},"pp":{"wt":"87–92"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92-48" id="mwAUc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAUg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUk">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAUo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAUs">However, terrace farming area makes up only about <span about="#mwt216" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"12"},"2":{"wt":"acre"},"3":{"wt":"ha"},"disp":{"wt":"flip"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAUw">4.9</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt216"> </span><span about="#mwt216">ha (12 acres)</span> of land, and a study of the soil around the terraces showed that what was grown there was mostly corn and potatoes, which was not enough to support more than 750 people living at Machu Picchu. This explains why studies done on the food that the Inca ate at Machu Picchu suggest it was imported from the surrounding valleys and farther afield.<sup about="#mwt217" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20125,_10_49-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20125, 10"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20125,_10-49"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Turner"},"2":{"wt":"Armelagos"},"3":{"wt":"2012"},"pp":{"wt":"5,10"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETurnerArmelagos20125,_10-49" id="mwAU0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAU4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAU8">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAVE">It is estimated that the area around the site has received more than <span about="#mwt220" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"1800"},"2":{"wt":"mm"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAVI">1,800</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt220"> </span><span about="#mwt220">mm (71</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt220"> </span><span about="#mwt220">in)</span> of rain per year since AD 1450, which was more than that needed to support crop growth. Because of this ample rainfall, routine <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Irrigation_in_Peru" title="Irrigation in Peru" id="mwAVM">irrigation</a> was generally unnecessary for the terraces. They received so much rain that they were built by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Incan_engineers" title="Incan engineers" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAVQ">Incan engineers</a> specifically to allow for drainage of excess water. Excavation and soil analyses done by Kenneth Wright<sup about="#mwt221" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWeingardt200890_50-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEWeingardt200890"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeingardt200890-50"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Weingardt"},"2":{"wt":"2008"},"p":{"wt":"90"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeingardt200890-50" id="mwAVU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAVY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVc">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt224" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrown2001_47-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBrown2001"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Brown"},"2":{"wt":"2001"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47" id="mwAVk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAVo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVs">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAVw">]</span></span></a></sup> in the 1990s showed that the terraces were built in layers, with a bottom layer of larger stones covered by loose gravel.<sup about="#mwt227" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrown2001_47-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBrown2001"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Brown"},"2":{"wt":"2001"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2001-47" id="mwAV0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAV4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAV8">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWA">]</span></span></a></sup> On top of the gravel was a layer of mixed sand and gravel packed together, with rich topsoil covering it. Research showed that the topsoil was probably moved from the valley floor to the terraces because it was much better than the soil higher up the mountain.<sup about="#mwt230" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar2004101_51-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar2004101"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar2004101-51"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"101"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar2004101-51" id="mwAWE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAWI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWM">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAWQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mwAWU"><h4 id="Rituals_and_offerings">Rituals and offerings</h4>\n<p id="mwAWY">In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_religion" title="Inca religion" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAWc">Inca religion</a>, human sacrifice, most prominently the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt233" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[capacocha]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAWg"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Capacocha" title="Capacocha">capacocha</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt233" id="mwAWk"/> ritual involving carefully selected, unblemished children, was practised at major <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt234" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[huaca]]s"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAWo"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Huaca" title="Huaca">huacas</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt234" id="mwAWs"/> on exceptional occasions to secure supernatural favour and to consolidate political and religious authority.<sup about="#mwt235" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMignone2018561–563_52-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMignone2018561–563"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMignone2018561–563-52"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Mignone"},"2":{"wt":"2018"},"pp":{"wt":"561–563"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMignone2018561–563-52" id="mwAWw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAW0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAW4">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAW8">]</span></span></a></sup> At Machu Picchu, however, there is little direct evidence for human sacrifice;<sup about="#mwt238" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGaitherKentSanchezTham2008114–116,_119_53-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEGaitherKentSanchezTham2008114–116, 119"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEGaitherKentSanchezTham2008114–116,_119-53"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Gaither"},"2":{"wt":"Kent"},"3":{"wt":"Sanchez"},"4":{"wt":"Tham"},"5":{"wt":"2008"},"pp":{"wt":"114–116,119"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGaitherKentSanchezTham2008114–116,_119-53" id="mwAXA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAXE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXI">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXM">]</span></span></a></sup> the archaeological record instead indicates that animal offerings, particularly <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Lama_(genus)" title="Lama (genus)" id="mwAXQ">camelids</a>, were common, with the Temple of the Condor and adjacent caves interpreted as sites for ritual sacrifice. Numerous camelid remains recovered at the site have been associated with funerary rituals and other ceremonial offerings.<sup about="#mwt241" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a72_54-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMillones2020a72"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a72-54"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Millones"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"p":{"wt":"72"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a72-54" id="mwAXU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAXY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXc">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt244" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200492–93_55-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200492–93"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200492–93-55"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"pp":{"wt":"92–93"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200492–93-55" id="mwAXk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAXo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXs">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAXw">]</span></span></a></sup> Excavations documented approximately 104 caves and rock shelters used as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Chamber_tomb" title="Chamber tomb" id="mwAX0">burial chambers</a> around Machu Picchu, containing the remains of about 174 individuals, interpreted as largely belonging to <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt247" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"yanaconas"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAX4"><i lang="qu">yanaconas</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt247" id="mwAX8"/> of diverse ethnic origins rather than the Inca elite.<sup about="#mwt248" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalazar2007167–185_56-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalazar2007167–185"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazar2007167–185-56"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salazar"},"2":{"wt":"2007"},"pp":{"wt":"167–185"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalazar2007167–185-56" id="mwAYA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAYE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYI">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAYM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="7" id="mwAYQ"><h3 id="Encounters_with_Westerners">Encounters with Westerners</h3>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAYU"><a href="./File:Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAYY"><img resource="./File:Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg/250px-Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg/500px-Machu_Picchu_and_the_Urubamba_Canyon.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Urubamba River canyon with Machu Picchu, Huayna Picchu and surrounding Andean peaks." data-file-width="3970" data-file-height="2499" data-file-type="bitmap" height="157" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAYc"/></a><figcaption id="mwAYg">A 1912 panoramic photograph of Machu Picchu and the Urubamba Canyon, taken during early Western exploration of the site.</figcaption></figure>\n\n<section data-mw-section-id="8" id="mwAYk"><h4 id="Spanish_conquest">Spanish conquest</h4>\n<p id="mwAYo">Machu Picchu is believed to have been abandoned in the mid-16th century, around the time of the Spanish conquest, likely due to the collapse of Inca rule and disease following European contact.<sup about="#mwt251" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200427_3-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200427"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200427-3"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"27"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200427-3" id="mwAYs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAYw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAY0">[</span>2<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAY4">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt254" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcNeill2010216_35-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMcNeill2010216"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNeill2010216-35"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"McNeill"},"2":{"wt":"2010"},"p":{"wt":"216"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNeill2010216-35" id="mwAY8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZE">[</span>32<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZI">]</span></span></a></sup> In the late 16th century, Spaniards who had gained control of the area documented that indigenous individuals mentioned returning to "Huayna Picchu", the name that is believed to be originally given to the site by locals.<sup about="#mwt257" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022_23-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado GonzalesBauer2022"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022-23"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amado Gonzales"},"2":{"wt":"Bauer"},"3":{"wt":"2022"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer2022-23" id="mwAZM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZU">[</span>20<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZY">]</span></span></a></sup> The Spanish conquistador <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Baltasar_de_Ocampo" title="Baltasar de Ocampo" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAZc">Baltasar de Ocampo</a> had notes of a visit during the end of the 16th century to a mountain fortress called <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt260" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Pitcos"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAZg"><i lang="es">Pitcos</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt260" id="mwAZk"/> with sumptuous and majestic buildings, erected with great skill and art, all the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Lintels" title="Lintels" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAZo">lintels</a> of the doors, as well the principal as the ordinary ones, being of marble and elaborately carved.<sup about="#mwt261" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDe_Ocampo199911_57-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDe Ocampo199911"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDe_Ocampo199911-57"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"De Ocampo"},"2":{"wt":"1999"},"page":{"wt":"11"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDe_Ocampo199911-57" id="mwAZs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZ0">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZ4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAZ8">Over the centuries, the surrounding jungle overgrew the site, and few outside the immediate area knew of its existence. The site may have been rediscovered and exploited in the late 19th century by the German engineer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Augusto_Berns" title="Augusto Berns" id="mwAaA">Augusto Berns</a>.<sup about="#mwt264" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_Gonzales2022528–533_58-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado Gonzales2022528–533"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_Gonzales2022528–533-58"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amado Gonzales"},"2":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"528–533"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_Gonzales2022528–533-58" id="mwAaE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAaI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaM">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Some suggest the German engineer J. M. von Hassel arrived earlier, though there's no solid evidence. Maps reference Machu Picchu as early as 1874, and a 1904 atlas labeled it as Huayna Picchu.<sup about="#mwt267" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBuck199327–29_59-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBuck199327–29"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuck199327–29-59"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Buck"},"2":{"wt":"1993"},"pp":{"wt":"27–29"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBuck199327–29-59" id="mwAaU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAaY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAac">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAag">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt270" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202221–24_60-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado GonzalesBauer202221–24"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202221–24-60"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amado Gonzales"},"2":{"wt":"Bauer"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"21–24"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202221–24-60" id="mwAak"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAao"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAas">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="9" id="mwAa0"><h4
