Lizárraga 1902" on a stone of the Temple of the Three Windows.' data-file-width="332" data-file-height="421" data-file-type="bitmap" height="157" width="124" class="mw-file-element"/></a></span></div></div></div><div class="trow" style="display:flex"><div class="thumbcaption">Inscription left by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Agustín_Lizárraga" title="Agustín Lizárraga">Agustín Lizárraga</a> in 1902 on the Temple of the Three Windows, marking the earliest known visit to Machu Picchu in modern times.<sup about="#mwt275" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202220–21_61-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmado GonzalesBauer202220–21"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202220–21-61"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmado_GonzalesBauer202220–21-61" id="mwAa8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbE">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbI">]</span></span></a></sup></div></div></div></div><span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt273"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Pages_using_multiple_image_with_auto_scaled_images"/><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Pages_using_multiple_image_with_unknown_parameters#position%20"/></span>\n<p id="mwAbM">In 1902, Peruvian explorer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Agustín_Lizárraga" title="Agustín Lizárraga" id="mwAbQ">Agustín Lizárraga</a> led an expedition to the area now known as Machu Picchu. After several hours of clearing undergrowth, they reached the stone structures of the citadel. During that visit, Lizárraga marked his surname and the year, "A. Lizárraga 1902", in charcoal on the central window of the Temple of the Three Windows. In 1911, American historian and explorer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Hiram_Bingham_III" title="Hiram Bingham III" id="mwAbU">Hiram Bingham</a> traveled the region looking for the lost capital of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Neo-Inca_state" title="Neo-Inca state" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAbY">Neo-Inca state</a> (later established to be <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Vilcabamba,_Peru" title="Vilcabamba, Peru" id="mwAbc">Vilcabamba</a>), established by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Manco_Inca" title="Manco Inca" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAbg">Manco Inca</a> after the Spanish conquest. They were led to Machu Picchu by a villager, Melchor Arteaga. Bingham found the surname of Lizárraga and the 1902 date on the temple. Initially disappointed, he documented in his pocket field journal: "Agustín Lizárraga is discoverer of Machu Picchu and lives at San Miguel Bridge just before passing."<sup about="#mwt277" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHeaney201183–96_62-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEHeaney201183–96"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeaney201183–96-62"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Heaney"},"2":{"wt":"2011"},"pp":{"wt":"83–96"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeaney201183–96-62" id="mwAbk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbs">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbw">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt280" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham1922219–226,_324_63-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham1922219–226, 324"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham1922219–226,_324-63"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"1922"},"pp":{"wt":"219–226, 324"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham1922219–226,_324-63" id="mwAb0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAb4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAb8">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcA">]</span></span></a></sup> However, while Bingham initially acknowledged Lizárraga as the discoverer in his early writings and speeches, including <i id="mwAcE">Inca Land</i> (1922), he gradually downplayed Lizárraga's role until, in his final version of the story, <i id="mwAcI">Lost City of the Incas</i> (1952), Bingham claimed to have found the site himself.<sup about="#mwt283" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHall201716–17_64-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEHall201716–17"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEHall201716–17-64"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Hall"},"2":{"wt":"2017"},"pp":{"wt":"16–17"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHall201716–17-64" id="mwAcM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcU">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcY">]</span></span></a></sup> In a 1922 letter to the head of the school he had once attended in Honolulu, Bingham wrote:<sup about="#mwt286" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham198925–26_65-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham198925–26"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham198925–26-65"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"1989"},"pp":{"wt":"25–26"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham198925–26-65" id="mwAcc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAck">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAco">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1244412712" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt289" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Template:Blockquote/styles.css"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Blockquote","href":"./Template:Blockquote"},"params":{"text":{"wt":"I suppose that in the same sense of the word as it is used in the expression \"Columbus discovered America\" it is fair to say that I discovered Machu Picchu. The Norsemen and the French fishermen undoubtedly visited North America long before Columbus crossed the Atlantic. On the other hand it was Columbus who made America known to the civilized world. In the same sense of the word I \"discovered\" Machu Picchu—in that before my visit and report on it it was not known to the geographical and historical societies in Peru, nor to the Peruvian government."}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAcs">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 32px}.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;margin-top:0}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{padding-left:1.6em}}</style><blockquote class="templatequote " about="#mwt289" id="mwAcw"><p>I suppose that in the same sense of the word as it is used in the expression "Columbus discovered America" it is fair to say that I discovered Machu Picchu. The Norsemen and the French fishermen undoubtedly visited North America long before Columbus crossed the Atlantic. On the other hand it was Columbus who made America known to the civilized world. In the same sense of the word I "discovered" Machu Picchu—in that before my visit and report on it it was not known to the geographical and historical societies in Peru, nor to the Peruvian government.</p></blockquote>\n\n<p id="mwAc0">Though Bingham was not the first to visit the ruins, he was considered the scientific discoverer who brought Machu Picchu to international attention. Bingham organized another expedition in 1912 to undertake major clearing and excavation.<sup about="#mwt291" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxx–xxxi_66-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxx–xxxi"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxx–xxxi-66"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"xxx–xxxi"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxx–xxxi-66" id="mwAc4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAc8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdA">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdE">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt294" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWiener20084–8_67-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEWiener20084–8"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiener20084–8-67"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Wiener"},"2":{"wt":"2008"},"pp":{"wt":"4–8"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWiener20084–8-67" id="mwAdI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdQ">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdU">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="10" id="mwAdY"><h4 id="1911_American_Expedition">1911 American Expedition</h4>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAdc"><a href="./File:Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAdg"><img resource="./File:Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg/250px-Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg/500px-Partial_view_of_Machu_Picchu_in_1911.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Black-and-white 1911 photograph showing a partial view of the ruins." data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="1586" data-file-type="bitmap" height="330" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAdk"/></a><figcaption id="mwAdo">Partial view of Machu Picchu on 24 July 1911, with much of the site covered by dense vegetation.</figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwAds">Bingham was a lecturer at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Yale_University" title="Yale University" id="mwAdw">Yale University</a>, although not a trained archaeologist. In 1909, returning from the Pan-American Scientific Congress in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Santiago" title="Santiago" id="mwAd0">Santiago</a>, he travelled through Peru. He was invited to explore the Inca ruins at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Choquequirao" title="Choquequirao" id="mwAd4">Choqquequirau</a> in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Department_of_Apurímac" title="Department of Apurímac" id="mwAd8">Apurímac Valley</a>. He organized the 1911 Yale Peruvian Expedition in part to search for the Inca capital, which was thought to be the city of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Vitcos" title="Vitcos" id="mwAeA">Vitcos</a>, reportedly located near the town of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Torontoy_(Peru)?action=edit&amp;redlink=1" title="Torontoy (Peru)" class="new" typeof="mw:LocalizedAttrs" data-mw-i18n='{"title":{"lang":"x-page","key":"red-link-title","params":["Torontoy (Peru)"]}}' id="mwAeE">Torontoy</a>.<sup about="#mwt297" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham1912174_68-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham1912174"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham1912174-68"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"1912"},"p":{"wt":"174"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham1912174-68" id="mwAeI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAeM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeQ">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeU">]</span></span></a></sup> He consulted Carlos Romero, one of the chief historians in Lima, who showed him helpful references and Father <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Antonio_de_la_Calancha" title="Antonio de la Calancha" id="mwAeY">Antonio de la Calancha</a>'s <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt300" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Corónica moralizada del Orden de San Agustín en el Perú"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAec"><i lang="es">Corónica moralizada del Orden de San Agustín en el Perú</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt300" id="mwAeg"/> (Chronicle of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Order_of_Saint_Augustine" title="Order of Saint Augustine" id="mwAek">Augustinians</a>), first published in 1631. In particular, Ramos thought Vitcos was "near a great white rock over a spring of fresh water." Back in Cusco again, Bingham asked planters about the places mentioned by Calancha, particularly along the Urubamba River. According to Bingham, "one old prospector said there were interesting ruins at Machu Picchu," though his statements "were given no importance by the leading citizens." Only later did Bingham learn that <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Charles_Wiener" title="Charles Wiener" id="mwAeo">Charles Wiener</a> had also heard of the ruins at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Huayna_Picchu" title="Huayna Picchu" id="mwAes">Huayna Picchu</a> and Machu Picchu, but was unable to reach them.<sup about="#mwt301" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2003112–135_69-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2003112–135"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003112–135-69"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"112–135"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003112–135-69" id="mwAew"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAe0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAe4">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAe8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt304" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37_70-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37-70"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"White"},"3":{"wt":"1983"},"p":{"wt":"S37"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37-70" id="mwAfA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAfE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfI">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAfQ">Armed with this information, Bingham's expedition went down the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Urubamba_River" title="Urubamba River" id="mwAfU">Urubamba River</a>. En route, Bingham asked local people to show them Inca ruins, especially any place described as having a white rock over a spring.<sup about="#mwt307" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2003137_71-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2003137"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003137-71"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"137"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003137-71" id="mwAfY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAfc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfg">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfk">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt310" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012387–389_72-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012387–389"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012387–389-72"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"MacQuarrie"},"2":{"wt":"2012"},"pp":{"wt":"387–389"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012387–389-72" id="mwAfo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAfs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfw">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAf0">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAf4">At Mandor Pampa, Bingham asked farmer and innkeeper Melchor Arteaga if he knew of any nearby ruins. Arteaga said he knew of excellent ruins on the top of Huayna Picchu.<sup about="#mwt313" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2010180–181_73-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2010180–181"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2010180–181-73"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2010"},"pp":{"wt":"180–181"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2010180–181-73" id="mwAf8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAgA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgE">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgI">]</span></span></a></sup> The next day, 24 July, Arteaga led Bingham and Sergeant Carrasco across the river on a log bridge and up to the Machu Picchu site. At the top of the mountain, they came across a small hut occupied by a couple of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Quechua_people" title="Quechua people" id="mwAgM">Quechua</a> people, Richarte and Alvarez, who were farming some of the original Machu Picchu agricultural terraces that they had cleared four years earlier. Richarte's 11-year-old son, Pablito, led Bingham along the ridge to the main ruins.<sup about="#mwt316" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20041_74-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEWrightValencia Zegarra20041"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20041-74"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Wright"},"2":{"wt":"Valencia Zegarra"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"1"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20041-74" id="mwAgQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAgU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgY">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAgg"><a href="./File:An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAgk"><img resource="./File:An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg/250px-An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg/500px-An_Architectural_Triumph_Machu_Picchu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Refer to caption" data-file-width="3072" data-file-height="1791" data-file-type="bitmap" height="146" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAgo"/></a><figcaption id="mwAgs">The Sacred Plaza, the Main Temple, and the Temple of the Three Windows after the 1912 clearing work. Above these structures is the Sacred Hill, which features the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Intihuatana,_Urubamba" title="Intihuatana, Urubamba" id="mwAgw">Intihuatana</a>.</figcaption></figure>\n\n<p id="mwAg0">The ruins were mostly covered with vegetation except for the cleared agricultural terraces and clearings used by the farmers as vegetable gardens. Because of the vegetation, Bingham was not able to observe the full extent of the site. He took preliminary notes, measurements, and photographs, noting the fine quality of the Inca stonework of several principal buildings. Bingham was unsure about the original purpose of the ruins, but concluded there was no indication that it matched the description of Vitcos.<sup about="#mwt319" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2003141,_186–187_75-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2003141, 186–187"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003141,_186–187-75"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"141, 186–187"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003141,_186–187-75" id="mwAg4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAg8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhA">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhE">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt322" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012255_76-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012255"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012255-76"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"MacQuarrie"},"2":{"wt":"2012"},"p":{"wt":"255"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacQuarrie2012255-76" id="mwAhI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAhM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhQ">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhU">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAhY">The expedition continued down the Urubamba and up the Vilcabamba Rivers, examining all the ruins they could find. Guided by locals, Bingham rediscovered and correctly identified the site of the old Inca capital, Vitcos (then called Rosaspata), and the nearby temple of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Chuquipalta" title="Chuquipalta" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAhc">Chuquipalta</a>. He then crossed a pass and into the Pampaconas Valley where he found more ruins heavily buried in the jungle undergrowth at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Espíritu_Pampa" title="Espíritu Pampa" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAhg">Espíritu Pampa</a>, which he named "Trombone Pampa".<sup about="#mwt325" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGeographical_Society_of_Philadelphia1912134–136_77-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEGeographical Society of Philadelphia1912134–136"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeographical_Society_of_Philadelphia1912134–136-77"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Geographical Society of Philadelphia"},"2":{"wt":"1912"},"pages":{"wt":"134–136"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeographical_Society_of_Philadelphia1912134–136-77" id="mwAhk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAho"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhs">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhw">]</span></span></a></sup> As was the case with Machu Picchu, the site was so heavily overgrown that Bingham could only note a few of the buildings. In 1964, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Gene_Savoy" title="Gene Savoy" id="mwAh0">Gene Savoy</a> further explored the ruins at Espiritu Pampa and revealed the full extent of the site, identifying it as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Vilcabamba,_Peru" title="Vilcabamba, Peru" id="mwAh4">Vilcabamba Viejo</a>, where the Incas fled after the Spanish drove them from Vitcos.<sup about="#mwt328" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200422–24_78-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200422–24"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200422–24-78"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"pp":{"wt":"22–24"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200422–24-78" id="mwAh8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAiA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiE">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiI">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt331" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxxv_79-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxxv"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxxv-79"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bingham"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"xxxv"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBingham2003xxxv-79" id="mwAiM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAiQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiU">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt334" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThomson2010282–286_80-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEThomson2010282–286"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomson2010282–286-80"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Thomson"},"2":{"wt":"2010"},"pp":{"wt":"282–286"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomson2010282–286-80" id="mwAic"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAig"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAik">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAio">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="11" id="mwAis"><h4 id="Excavations_and_controversy_(1912–1915)"><span id="Excavations_and_controversy_.281912.E2.80.931915.29" typeof="mw:FallbackId"></span>Excavations and controversy (1912–1915)</h4>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAiw"><a href="./File:Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAi0"><img resource="./File:Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg/250px-Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg/500px-Map_of_the_Peruvian_Expedition_of_1912.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Map showing routes of the 1912 Peruvian expedition, with four topographic surveys areas." data-file-width="2758" data-file-height="2347" data-file-type="bitmap" height="213" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAi4"/></a><figcaption id="mwAi8">Route map of the 1912 Yale Peruvian Expedition, which carried out the first archaeological excavations at Machu Picchu.<sup about="#mwt337" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022273_81-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022273"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022273-81"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Capozzoli"},"2":{"wt":"Romano"},"3":{"wt":"Sileo"},"4":{"wt":"Lasaponara"},"5":{"wt":"2022"},"p":{"wt":"273"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022273-81" id="mwAjA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAjE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjI">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjM">]</span></span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwAjQ">Bingham returned to Machu Picchu in 1912 under the sponsorship of Yale University and the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./National_Geographic_Society" title="National Geographic Society" id="mwAjU">National Geographic Society</a>. The expedition conducted site clearing and archaeological work between July and November of that year, under the supervision of George Eaton and Ellwood Erdis. These efforts included burnings, vegetation removal, mapping, and excavations, many of which were carried out with the assistance of local labor organized in part by Ángel Lizárraga, younger brother of Agustín Lizárraga. The work was supported logistically by regional authorities, including the Prefect of Cusco. Excavations resumed in 1914 and 1915 during a subsequent expedition. Although Bingham proposed several hypotheses regarding the purpose and significance of the site, none have been substantiated by later research. During the expeditions, numerous artifacts were recovered and transported to Yale University. Among these was a set of 15th-century ceremonial Incan knives made from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Bismuth_bronze" title="Bismuth bronze" id="mwAjY">bismuth bronze</a>, which are the earliest known artifacts to contain this alloy.<sup about="#mwt340" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a25–39_82-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBastante2020a25–39"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a25–39-82"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bastante"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"25–39"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a25–39-82" id="mwAjc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAjg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjk">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjo">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt343" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGordonRutledge1984585_83-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEGordonRutledge1984585"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordonRutledge1984585-83"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Gordon"},"2":{"wt":"Rutledge"},"3":{"wt":"1984"},"p":{"wt":"585"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGordonRutledge1984585-83" id="mwAjs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAjw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAj0">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAj4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAj8">Although local institutions initially welcomed the exploration, they soon accused Bingham of legal and cultural malpractice.<sup about="#mwt346" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370_84-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalvatore200370"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370-84"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salvatore"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"p":{"wt":"70"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370-84" id="mwAkA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkI">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkM">]</span></span></a></sup> Rumors arose that the team was stealing artifacts and smuggling them out of Peru through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Bolivia" title="Bolivia" id="mwAkQ">Bolivia</a>. In fact, Bingham removed many artifacts, but openly and legally; they were deposited in the Yale University Museum. Bingham was abiding by the 1852 Civil Code of Peru; the code stated that "archaeological finds generally belonged to the discoverer, except when they had been discovered on private land".<sup about="#mwt349" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBatievskyVelarde2006100_85-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBatievskyVelarde2006100"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBatievskyVelarde2006100-85"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Batievsky"},"2":{"wt":"Velarde"},"3":{"wt":"2006"},"p":{"wt":"100"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBatievskyVelarde2006100-85" id="mwAkU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkc">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkg">]</span></span></a></sup> Local press perpetuated the accusations, claiming that the excavation harmed the site and deprived local archaeologists of knowledge about their own history. Landowners began to demand rent from the excavators.<sup about="#mwt352" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370_84-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalvatore200370"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370-84"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salvatore"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"p":{"wt":"70"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370-84" id="mwAkk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAko"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAks">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkw">]</span></span></a></sup> By the time Bingham and his team left Machu Picchu, locals had formed coalitions to defend their ownership of Machu Picchu and its cultural remains, while Bingham claimed the artifacts ought to be studied by experts in American institutions.<sup about="#mwt355" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370–71_86-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESalvatore200370–71"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370–71-86"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Salvatore"},"2":{"wt":"2003"},"pp":{"wt":"70–71"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalvatore200370–71-86" id="mwAk0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAk4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAk8">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAlA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="12" id="mwAlE"><h4 id="Dispute_over_cultural_artifacts">Dispute over cultural artifacts</h4>\n<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt358" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Peru–Yale University dispute"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAlI"><style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1368532237" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" about="#mwt359" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}'>.mw-parser-output .hatnote{font-style:italic}.mw-parser-output div.hatnote{padding-left:1.6em;margin-bottom:0.5em}.mw-parser-output .hatnote i{font-style:normal}.mw-parser-output .hatnote+.mw-empty-elt+.hatnote{margin-top:-0.5em}@media print{body.ns-0 .mw-parser-output .hatnote{display:none!important}}</style></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt358" id="mwAlM">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Peru–Yale_University_dispute" title="Peru–Yale University dispute">Peru–Yale University dispute</a></div>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAlQ"><a 2x" alt="Ancient clay pots of different shapes and sizes displayed on white stepped stands." data-file-width="2784" data-file-height="1847" data-file-type="bitmap" height="166" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAlY"/></a><figcaption id="mwAlc"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_Empire#Ceramics,_precious_metals_and_textiles" title="Inca Empire" id="mwAlg">Aryballos and bowls</a> part of the first batch of thousands of Machu Picchu artifacts returned by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Yale_University" title="Yale University" id="mwAlk">Yale University</a> in 2011.</figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwAlo">In 1912, 1914, and 1915, Bingham removed thousands of artifacts from Machu Picchu—ceramic vessels, silver statues, jewelry, and human bones—and took them to Yale University for further study, supposedly for 18 months. Yale instead kept the artifacts until 2012, arguing that Peru lacked the infrastructure and systems to care for them. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Eliane_Karp" title="Eliane Karp" id="mwAls">Eliane Karp</a>, an anthropologist and wife of former Peruvian President <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Alejandro_Toledo" title="Alejandro Toledo" id="mwAlw">Alejandro Toledo</a>, accused Yale of profiting from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cultural_heritage_of_Peru" title="Cultural heritage of Peru" id="mwAl0">Peru's cultural heritage</a>. Many of the articles were exhibited at Yale's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History" title="Peabody Museum of Natural History" id="mwAl4">Peabody Museum</a>.<sup about="#mwt360" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESwanson2009471–491_87-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESwanson2009471–491"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESwanson2009471–491-87"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Swanson"},"2":{"wt":"2009"},"pp":{"wt":"471–491"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESwanson2009471–491-87" id="mwAl8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmE">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwAmM">In 2006, Yale returned some pieces but retained more than 250 "museum-quality" pieces, claiming this was supported by federal case law of Peruvian antiquities.<sup about="#mwt369" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-88" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-88"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-88" id="mwAmQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmY">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmc">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2007, the Peruvian government and Yale had agreed on a joint traveling exhibition and construction of a new museum and research center in Cusco advised by Yale. Yale acknowledged Peru's title to all the objects, but would share rights with Peru in the research collection, part of which would remain at Yale for continuing study.<sup about="#mwt372" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-89" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-89"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-89" id="mwAmg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmo">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAms">]</span></span></a></sup> In November 2010, Yale agreed to return the disputed artifacts.<sup about="#mwt375" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-90" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-90"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-90" id="mwAmw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAm0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAm4">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAm8">]</span></span></a></sup> The third and final batch of artifacts was delivered in November 2012.<sup about="#mwt378" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-91" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-91"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-91" id="mwAnA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAnE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnI">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnM">]</span></span></a></sup> The artifacts are permanently exhibited at the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Casa_Concha" title="Casa Concha" id="mwAnQ">Machu Picchu Museum</a>–<span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt363" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Casa Concha"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwAnU"><i lang="es">Casa Concha</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt363" id="mwAnY"/>, located near Cusco's colonial center and owned by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./National_University_of_Saint_Anthony_the_Abbot_in_Cuzco" title="National University of Saint Anthony the Abbot in Cuzco" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAnc">National University of San Antonio Abad del Cusco</a>.<sup about="#mwt364" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a39–42,_54_92-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBastante2020a39–42, 54"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a39–42,_54-92"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bastante"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"39–42, 54"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a39–42,_54-92" id="mwAng"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAnk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAno">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAns">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="13" id="mwAnw"><h4 id="Later_archaeological_research_and_scientific_studies">Later archaeological research and scientific studies</h4>\n<p id="mwAn0">After Bingham's expeditions, state and institutional projects carried out mainly restoration and limited excavations between 1929 and 1971. From the 1970s to the 1990s, a series of targeted excavations and conservation programs recovered mainly <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_Empire#Ceramics,_precious_metals_and_textiles" title="Inca Empire" id="mwAn4">Inca artifacts</a> (ceramics, stone tools, and metal objects). They documented disturbed or reworked layers within the site. Between 2014 and 2017, the Archaeological and Interdisciplinary Research Program in the Historic Sanctuary of Machupicchu (PIAISHM) carried out systematic excavations, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Pollen_analysis" title="Pollen analysis" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAn8">pollen studies</a>, and architectural analyses that clarified construction phases, recorded offerings, and refined interpretations of its function and population.<sup about="#mwt379" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBastanteAsteteFernándezUsca2020a166–221_93-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBastanteAsteteFernándezUsca2020a166–221"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastanteAsteteFernándezUsca2020a166–221-93"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Bastante"},"2":{"wt":"Astete"},"3":{"wt":"Fernández"},"4":{"wt":"Usca"},"5":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"166–221"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBastanteAsteteFernándezUsca2020a166–221-93" id="mwAoA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAoE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoI">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoM">]</span></span></a></sup> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Radiocarbon_dating" title="Radiocarbon dating" id="mwAoQ">Radiocarbon dating</a> analyses have refined the site's chronology, indicating that Machu Picchu’s main construction and use fall in the early to mid 15th century, slightly earlier than some traditional documentary chronologies suggest.<sup about="#mwt382" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273_16-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273-16"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"Nesbitt"},"4":{"wt":"Washburn"},"5":{"wt":"2021"},"p":{"wt":"1273"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazarNesbittWashburn20211273-16" id="mwAoU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAoY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoc">[</span>14<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAog">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt385" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiBastanteHoggSieczkowska20211146_27-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiBastanteHoggSieczkowska20211146"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiBastanteHoggSieczkowska20211146-27"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Ziółkowski"},"2":{"wt":"Bastante"},"3":{"wt":"Hogg"},"4":{"wt":"Sieczkowska"},"5":{"wt":"2021"},"pp":{"wt":"1146"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiBastanteHoggSieczkowska20211146-27" id="mwAok"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAoo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAos">[</span>24<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAow">]</span></span></a></sup>\nBetween 2017 and 2019, an international team led by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Nicola_Masini" title="Nicola Masini" id="mwAo0">Nicola Masini</a> of Italy’s CNR investigated the Principal Plaza using archaeological, remote-sensing, and geophysical data. The study found that the area evolved from a natural drainage basin to a quarry before being reshaped with subsurface drainage. The plaza was likely built in at least two phases, beginning as a smaller sunken plaza (plaza hundida) that was later raised and expanded into the present ceremonial space.<sup about="#mwt389" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-94" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-94"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-94" id="mwAo4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAo8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApA">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApE">]</span></span></a></sup><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_minor_POV_problems_from_August_2026" about="#mwt388" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Undue weight inline","href":"./Template:Undue_weight_inline"},"params":{"date":{"wt":"August 2026"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwApI"/><sup class="noprint Inline-Template " style="white-space:nowrap;" about="#mwt388" id="mwApM"><span typeof="mw:Entity">[</span><i><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view#Due_and_undue_weight" title="Wikipedia:Neutral point of view"><span title="The material near this tag may be giving undue weight to a viewpoint or idea. (August 2026)">undue weight?</span></a><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span><span typeof="mw:Entity">–</span> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Talk:Machu_Picchu#undue" title="Talk:Machu Picchu">discuss</a></i><span typeof="mw:Entity">]</span></sup></p>\n\n</section></section></section><section data-mw-section-id="14" id="mwApQ"><h2 id="Current_state">Current state</h2>\n<section id="mwArA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwArE">Beyond its historical significance, Machu Picchu houses a diverse range of species. Among them are the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Culpeo" title="Culpeo" id="mwArI">Andean fox</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cougar" title="Cougar" id="mwArM">puma</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Vizcacha" title="Vizcacha" class="mw-redirect" id="mwArQ">vizcacha</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Spectacled_bear" title="Spectacled bear" id="mwArU">spectacled bear</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./White-tailed_deer" title="White-tailed deer" id="mwArY">white-tailed deer</a>. The sanctuary is also a habitat for more than 420 bird species, such as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cock-of-the-rock" title="Cock-of-the-rock" id="mwArc">cock-of-the-rock</a> and the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Andean_condor" title="Andean condor" id="mwArg">Andean condor</a>. The area hosts over 550 tree species across 74 families, including ferns, gymnosperms, and palms.<sup about="#mwt402" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOchoa2020b379–390_98-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" Heritage Site</a>, describing it as "a masterpiece of art, urbanism, architecture and engineering" and "a unique testimony" of the Inca civilization, with the inscription covering both the archaeological complex and its surrounding landscape.<sup about="#mwt407" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-unesco_99-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" id="mwAu8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvE">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvI">]</span></span></a></sup> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Tinúm_Municipality" title="Tinúm Municipality" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAvM">Tinum</a>, Mexico.<sup about="#mwt433" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-107" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-107"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-107" id="mwAvQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvY">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="17" id="mwAvg"><h3 id="Tourist_activity">Tourist activity</h3>\n<p id="mwAvk">Machu Picchu is both a cultural and natural <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site" title="UNESCO World Heritage Site" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAvo">UNESCO World Heritage Site</a>. Since Hiram Bingham's expedition, growing numbers of tourists have visited the site each year, with numbers exceeding 1.5 million in 2025.<sup about="#mwt434" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60_108-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table No. 60"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60-108"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"MINCETUR"},"2":{"wt":"2026"},"loc":{"wt":"Table No. 60"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60-108" id="mwAvs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv0">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv4">]</span></span></a></sup> As Peru's most visited tourist attraction and a major revenue generator, it is continually exposed to economic and commercial forces. In the late 1990s, the Peruvian government granted concessions to allow the construction of a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cable_car_(railway)" title="Cable car (railway)" id="mwAv8">cable car</a> and a luxury hotel, including a tourist complex with boutiques and restaurants and a bridge to the site.<sup about="#mwt442" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-BBC1_109-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"BBC1"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-BBC1-109"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-BBC1-109" id="mwAwA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwI">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwM">]</span></span></a></sup> These plans faced widespread protests, with critics arguing that the government had failed to conduct a proper environmental impact survey, as requested by the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./National_Institute_of_Natural_Resources" title="National Institute of Natural Resources" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAwQ">National Institute of Natural Resources</a>, which warned of potential harm to the ecosystem.<sup about="#mwt437" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMedrano199813_110-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMedrano199813"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedrano199813-110"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Medrano"},"2":{"wt":"1998"},"p":{"wt":"13"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedrano199813-110" id="mwAwU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwc">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwg">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2018, plans were restarted to construct a cable car again to encourage Peruvians to visit Machu Picchu and boost domestic tourism.<sup about="#mwt445" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-111" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-111"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-111" id="mwAwk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAws">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAww">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt448" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-112" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-112"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-112" id="mwAw0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAw4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAw8">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxA">]</span></span></a></sup> A <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./No-fly_zone" title="No-fly zone" id="mwAxE">no-fly zone</a> exists above the area.<sup about="#mwt451" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-ban_113-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"ban"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-ban-113"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-ban-113" id="mwAxI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAxM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxQ">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxU">]</span></span></a></sup> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./UNESCO" title="UNESCO" id="mwAxY">UNESCO</a> considered including Machu Picchu on its <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger" title="List of World Heritage in Danger" id="mwAxc">List of World Heritage in Danger</a> in 2017 due to overcrowding concerns, but ultimately decided against it.<sup about="#mwt454" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-114" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-114"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-114" id="mwAxg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAxk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxo">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxs">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt457" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-115" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-115"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-115" id="mwAxw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAx0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAx4">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAx8">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAyA"><a href="./File:Machu_Picchu_Gate.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAyE"><img resource="./File:Machu_Picchu_Gate.jpg" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Machu_Picchu_Gate.jpg/250px-Machu_Picchu_Gate.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAyI"/></a><figcaption id="mwAyM">Tourists entering Machu Picchu, which received over 1.5 million visitors in 2025 (about 4,100 per day), a fourfold increase since 2000.<sup about="#mwt458" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBaumhackl2019107–108_116-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBaumhackl2019107–108"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaumhackl2019107–108-116"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Baumhackl"},"2":{"wt":"2019"},"pp":{"wt":"107–108"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaumhackl2019107–108-116" id="mwAyQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAyU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyY">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyc">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt461" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60_108-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table No. 60"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60-108"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"MINCETUR"},"2":{"wt":"2026"},"loc":{"wt":"Table No. 60"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._60-108" id="mwAyg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAyk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyo">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAys">]</span></span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>\n\n<p id="mwAyw">Efforts to manage the impact of tourism have included various measures over the years. In the 1980s, a rock from Machu Picchu's central plaza was moved to create a helicopter landing zone, a practice that was later stopped. In 2006, the company Helicusco sought approval for tourist flights over the site, but the license was soon rescinded.<sup about="#mwt467" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-ban_113-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"ban"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-ban-113" id="mwAy0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAy4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAy8">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzA">]</span></span></a></sup> In January 2010, severe flooding caused by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./El_Niño–Southern_Oscillation" title="El Niño–Southern Oscillation" id="mwAzE">El Niño</a> trapped over 4,000 people and disrupted access to Machu Picchu, leading to its temporary closure.<sup about="#mwt470" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-117" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-117"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-117" id="mwAzI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAzM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzQ">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzU">]</span></span></a></sup> The site reopened on April 1, 2010.<sup about="#mwt473" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-118" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-118"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-118" id="mwAzY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAzc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzg">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzk">]</span></span></a></sup> To further address tourism's impact, stricter entrance regulations were introduced in July 2011, limiting the number of daily visitors to 2,500 per day to the citadel.<sup about="#mwt464" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELarsonPoudyal2012925_119-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTELarsonPoudyal2012925"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTELarsonPoudyal2012925-119"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Larson"},"2":{"wt":"Poudyal"},"3":{"wt":"2012"},"pp":{"wt":"925"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELarsonPoudyal2012925-119" id="mwAzo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAzs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzw">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAz0">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2018, a new entrance system was added to manage tourism better and reduce site degradation.<sup about="#mwt476" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-120" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-120"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-120" id="mwAz4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAz8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0A">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0E">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2024, the daily visitor limit was officially increased to 4,500, with up to 5,600 permitted during peak season.<sup about="#mwt479" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-121" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-121"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-121" id="mwA0I"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA0M"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0Q">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0U">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt482" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-122" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-122"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-122" id="mwA0Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA0c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0g">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0k">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwA0o">In May 2012, UNESCO urged additional protection measures for the site's buffer zone, especially due to the rapid growth in the nearby town of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Aguas_Calientes,_Peru" title="Aguas Calientes, Peru" id="mwA0s">Aguas Calientes</a>.<sup about="#mwt488" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-123" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-123"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-123" id="mwA0w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA00"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA04">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA08">]</span></span></a></sup> Tourist deaths at Machu Picchu from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Altitude_sickness" title="Altitude sickness" id="mwA1A">altitude sickness</a>, floods, and accidents have led to criticism of UNESCO for allowing visits despite the site's high safety risks.<sup about="#mwt491" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-124" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-124"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-124" id="mwA1E"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1I"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1M">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1Q">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt494" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-125" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-125"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-125" id="mwA1U"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1Y"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1c">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1g">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt497" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-126" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-126"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-126" id="mwA1k"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1o"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1s">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1w">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt483" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKeough2011608_127-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEKeough2011608"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeough2011608-127"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Keough"},"2":{"wt":"2011"},"pp":{"wt":"608"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKeough2011608-127" id="mwA10"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA14"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA18">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2A">]</span></span></a></sup> The trend of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Nude_recreation" title="Nude recreation" id="mwA2E">nude tourism</a> in 2014 also led to increased surveillance by Peru's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ministry_of_Culture_(Peru)" title="Ministry of Culture (Peru)" id="mwA2I">Ministry of Culture</a> to end the practice.<sup about="#mwt500" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-128" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-128"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-128" id="mwA2M"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA2Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2U">[</span>125<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2Y">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwA2c">In recognition of efforts to manage and protect the site, Fernando Astete, who served as Chief of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./National_Archaeological_Park_of_Machu_Picchu" title="National Archaeological Park of Machu Picchu" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA2g">National Archaeological Park of Machu Picchu</a> from 1994 to 2019, was honored with the "Personalidad Meritoria de la Cultura" award by the Ministry of Culture of Peru in January 2020. This award acknowledged his extensive contributions to the preservation, management, and study of Machu Picchu.<sup about="#mwt503" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-129" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-129"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-129" id="mwA2k"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA2o"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2s">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2w">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt506" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-130" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-130"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-130" id="mwA20"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA24"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA28">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3A">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwA3E">Machu Picchu was closed to visitors in March 2020 because of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./COVID-19_pandemic_in_Peru" title="COVID-19 pandemic in Peru" id="mwA3I">COVID-19 pandemic</a>. In October 2020, the site was briefly opened to allow one stranded Japanese tourist to visit.<sup about="#mwt509" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-131" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-131"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-131" id="mwA3M"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA3Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3U">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3Y">]</span></span></a></sup> It reopened in November 2020 after an eight-month shutdown, the initial reopening limited admissions to 675 visitors per day under strict biosafety protocols.<sup about="#mwt512" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-132" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-132"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-132" id="mwA3c"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA3g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3k">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3o">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt515" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-133" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-133"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-133" id="mwA3s"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA3w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA30">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA34">]</span></span></a></sup> During the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./2022–2023_Peruvian_protests" title="2022–2023 Peruvian protests" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA38">2022–2023 Peruvian protests</a>, routes to Machu Picchu were blocked, trapping thousands of tourists and leading to a government airlift of the stranded visitors.<sup about="#mwt518" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-:4_134-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":":4"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-:4-134"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-:4-134" id="mwA4A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA4E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4I">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4M">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt521" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-135" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-135"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-135" id="mwA4Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA4U"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4Y">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4c">]</span></span></a></sup> Due to these disruptions, the Ministry of Culture closed the site indefinitely on 22 January 2023. It was reopened on 15 February 2023.<sup about="#mwt522" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-:4_134-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":":4"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-:4-134" id="mwA4g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA4k"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4o">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4s">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt525" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-dw.com_136-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"dw.com"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-dw.com-136"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-dw.com-136" id="mwA4w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA40"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA44">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA48">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt528" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-137" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-137"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-137" id="mwA5A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA5E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5I">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5M">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="18" id="mwA5Q"><h2 id="Geography">Geography</h2>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwA5U"><a It is one of the most important archaeological sites in South America, one of the most visited tourist attractions in Latin America, and the most visited in Peru.<sup about="#mwt539" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDavies1997163_139-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDavies1997163"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies1997163-139"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Davies"},"2":{"wt":"1997"},"p":{"wt":"163"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavies1997163-139" id="mwA6s"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA6w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA60">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA64">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwA68">Machu Picchu is situated above a bow of the Urubamba River, which surrounds the site on three sides, where cliffs drop vertically for <span about="#mwt542" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"450"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"ft"},"sp":{"wt":"us"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwA7A">450 meters (1,480</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt542"> </span><span about="#mwt542">ft)</span> to the river at their base. was intentionally kept secret and served as an imperial refuge for Inca elites.<sup about="#mwt546" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBuse197842–43_140-0" rel="dc:references" Constructed with stone retaining walls and well-drained topsoil, the terraces were built using deeper strata and stone chips to enhance drainage and ensure stability.<sup about="#mwt559" class="mw-ref class="mw-redirect" id="mwA-c">earthquake faults</a>. According to research conducted in 2019, this may not be a coincidence: "[o]ne simple answer, researchers now suggest, is that that's [earthquake faults] where building materials for the site—large amounts of already fractured rock—were readily available."<sup about="#mwt574" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-147" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-147"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-147" id="mwA-g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA-k"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-o">[</span>144<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-s">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<section data-mw-section-id="19" id="mwA-w"><h3 id="Climate">Climate</h3>\n<p id="mwA-0">Between the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Sacred_Valley" title="Sacred Valley" id="mwA-4">valley floor</a> and the altitudinal zone of the Inca citadel, ranging from <span about="#mwt575" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2200"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"ft"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwA-8">2,200 metres (7,200</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt575"> </span><span about="#mwt575">ft)</span> to <span about="#mwt576" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2500"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"ft"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwA_A">2,500 metres (8,200</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt576"> </span><span about="#mwt576">ft)</span> meters above sea level, Machu Picchu features a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Subtropical_highland_climate" title="Subtropical highland climate" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_E">subtropical highland climate</a>, with an average annual precipitation of <span about="#mwt577" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2010"},"2":{"wt":"mm"},"3":{"wt":"in"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwA_I">2,010 millimetres (79</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt577"> </span><span about="#mwt577">in)</span> and an annual mean temperature of approximately <span about="#mwt578" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"18"},"2":{"wt":"C"},"3":{"wt":"F"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwA_M">18</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt578"> </span><span about="#mwt578">°C (64</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt578"> </span><span about="#mwt578">°F)</span>. The site is characterized by steep slopes, dense vegetation, and significant rainfall, contributing to high humidity levels of 80–90%. The area is also frequently enveloped in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cloud_cover" title="Cloud cover" id="mwA_Q">cloud cover</a>, typical of a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Cloud_forest" title="Cloud forest" id="mwA_U">cloud forest</a> environment.<sup about="#mwt579" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201519–24_148-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion
