id="mwBAo">The site is divided into two main sectors: an agricultural sector to the southeast composed of terraces (<span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt593" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"andenes"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBAs"><i lang="es">andenes</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt593" id="mwBAw"/>), and an urban sector to the northeast containing residences, places of worship, and warehouses. The urban sector is further split into an upper town (<span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt594" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Hanan"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBA0"><i lang="qu">Hanan</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt594" id="mwBA4"/>) and a lower town (<span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt595" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Hurin"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBA8"><i lang="qu">Hurin</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt595" id="mwBBA"/>).<sup about="#mwt596" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022272–275_150-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022272–275"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022272–275-150"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Capozzoli"},"2":{"wt":"Romano"},"3":{"wt":"Sileo"},"4":{"wt":"Lasaponara"},"5":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"272–275"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022272–275-150" id="mwBBE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBM">[</span>147<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBQ">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBBU">The <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt599" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Hanan"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBBY"><i lang="qu">Hanan</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt599" id="mwBBc"/> contains the Sacred Plaza (<span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt600" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Plaza Sagrada"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBBg"><i lang="es">Plaza Sagrada</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt600" id="mwBBk"/>), a courtyard complex incorporating the Main Temple and the Temple of the Three Windows and capped by a pyramid-like stone platform on which the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt601" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[Intihuatana, Urubamba|Intihuatana]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBBo"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Intihuatana,_Urubamba" title="Intihuatana, Urubamba">Intihuatana</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt601" id="mwBBs"/> stands. In contrast, the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt602" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Hurin"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBBw"><i lang="qu">Hurin</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt602" id="mwBB0"/> is marked by trapezoidal doorways and small rectangular <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt603" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[Inca kancha|kanchas]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBB4"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_kancha" title="Inca kancha">kanchas</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt603" id="mwBB8"/>, including three large, symmetrically arranged kanchas with housing and workshops overlooking the Main Square (<span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt604" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Plaza Principal"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBCA"><i lang="es">Plaza Principal</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt604" id="mwBCE"/>), and a large single-entrance building interpreted as an <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt605" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"[[Acllahuasi]]"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBCI"><i lang="qu"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Acllahuasi" title="Acllahuasi" class="mw-redirect">Acllahuasi</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt605" id="mwBCM"/>; nearby is the Temple of the Condor, which includes ritual caves and a large carved stone often interpreted as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Condor" title="Condor" id="mwBCQ">condor</a>.<sup about="#mwt606" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022274–275_151-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022274–275"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022274–275-151"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Capozzoli"},"2":{"wt":"Romano"},"3":{"wt":"Sileo"},"4":{"wt":"Lasaponara"},"5":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"274–275"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTECapozzoliRomanoSileoLasaponara2022274–275-151" id="mwBCU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBCY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCc">[</span>148<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBCk">The architecture is adapted to the mountains. Approximately 200 buildings are arranged on wide parallel terraces around an east–west central square. The various compounds, called <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt609" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"kanchas"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBCo"><i lang="qu">kanchas</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt609" id="mwBCs"/>, are long and narrow in order to exploit the terrain. Sophisticated channeling systems provided irrigation for the fields. Stone stairways set in the walls allowed access to the different levels across the site. The eastern section of the city was probably residential. The western section, separated by the square, was for religious and ceremonial purposes. This section contains the <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt610" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Torreón"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBCw"><i lang="es">Torreón</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt610" id="mwBC0"/>, the massive tower which may have been used as an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Observatory" title="Observatory" id="mwBC4">observatory</a>.<sup about="#mwt611" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELonghenaAlva2007252_152-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTELonghenaAlva2007252"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTELonghenaAlva2007252-152"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Longhena"},"2":{"wt":"Alva"},"3":{"wt":"2007"},"p":{"wt":"252"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELonghenaAlva2007252-152" id="mwBC8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBDA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDE">[</span>149<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBDM">Located in the urban sector are the primary archaeological treasures and tourist attractions: the <i id="mwBDQ"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Intihuatana,_Urubamba" title="Intihuatana, Urubamba" id="mwBDU">Intihuatana</a></i>, the <i id="mwBDY">Temple of the Sun,</i> and the <i id="mwBDc">Temple of the Three Windows</i>.<sup about="#mwt614" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67_153-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67-153"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Millones"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"p":{"wt":"67"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67-153" id="mwBDg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBDk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDo">[</span>150<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDs">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBDw">The Popular District, or Residential District, is the place where the lower-class people live. It includes storage buildings and simple houses.<sup about="#mwt617" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAsteteBastante2020b226_154-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAsteteBastante2020b226"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAsteteBastante2020b226-154"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Astete"},"2":{"wt":"Bastante"},"3":{"wt":"2020b"},"p":{"wt":"226"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAsteteBastante2020b226-154" id="mwBD0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBD4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBD8">[</span>151<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEA">]</span></span></a></sup> The Guardian's house is a three-sided building, with one of its long sides opening onto the Terrace of the Ceremonial Rock. The three-sided style of Inca architecture is known as the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt620" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"wayrona"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBEE"><i lang="qu">wayrona</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt620" id="mwBEI"/> style.<sup about="#mwt621" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20048_155-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEWrightValencia Zegarra20048"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20048-155"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Wright"},"2":{"wt":" Valencia Zegarra"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"8"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra20048-155" id="mwBEM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBEQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEU">[</span>152<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEY">]</span></span></a></sup> In 2005 and 2009, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./University_of_Arkansas" title="University of Arkansas" id="mwBEc">University of Arkansas</a> made detailed <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./3d_laser_scanning" title="3d laser scanning" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBEg">laser scans</a> of the entire site and of the ruins at the top of the adjacent Huayna Picchu mountain. The scan data is available online for research purposes.<sup about="#mwt626" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-156" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-156"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-156" id="mwBEk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBEo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEs">[</span>153<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="22" id="mwBE0"><h3 id="Sites_of_interest">Sites of interest</h3>\n<section data-mw-section-id="23" id="mwBE4"><h4 id="Temple_of_the_Sun_or_Torreón"><span id="Temple_of_the_Sun_or_Torre.C3.B3n" typeof="mw:FallbackId"></span>Temple of the Sun or Torreón</h4>\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBE8"><a href="./File:Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBFA"><img resource="./File:Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG" src="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG/330px-Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail" decoding="async" loading="lazy" srcset="//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG/960px-Machupicchu_intihuatana.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&amp;utm_campaign=parser&amp;utm_content=thumbnail 2x" alt="Temple of the Sun with stone structures and a backdrop of mountains." data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" data-file-type="bitmap" height="225" width="300" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.2" id="mwBFE"/></a><figcaption id="mwBFI">Temple of the Sun (<span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt627" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Torreón"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBFM"><i lang="es">Torreón</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt627" id="mwBFQ"/>), a two-part ashlar structure in the upper town, with carved platforms and solar-aligned openings</figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwBFU">The <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt628" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Torreón"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBFY"><i lang="es">Torreón</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt628" id="mwBFc"/> is a semicircular, two-part structure built among the large granite blocks in the upper town (<span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt629" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Hanan"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBFg"><i lang="qu">Hanan</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt629" id="mwBFk"/>), within the urban sector of Machu Picchu. It occupies the rock overlying Bingham’s "Royal Mausoleum" and, like the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Coricancha" title="Coricancha" id="mwBFo">Coricancha</a> at Cusco and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Pisac" title="Pisac" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBFs">Pisac</a>, has been described as having a "parabolic enclosure wall".<sup about="#mwt630" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45_157-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45-157"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"White"},"3":{"wt":"1983"},"pp":{"wt":"S37-S45"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45-157" id="mwBFw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBF0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBF4">[</span>154<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBF8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt633" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKrupp199447–51_158-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEKrupp199447–51"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrupp199447–51-158"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Krupp"},"2":{"wt":"1994"},"pages":{"wt":"47–51"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrupp199447–51-158" id="mwBGA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBGE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGI">[</span>155<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGM">]</span></span></a></sup> The lower part fills an irregular, cave-like space between wedged boulders. It contains fine <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ashlar_masonry" title="Ashlar masonry" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBGQ">ashlar masonry</a> with several trapezoidal <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Niche_(architecture)" title="Niche (architecture)" id="mwBGU">niches</a>; in some places, the natural rock was worked into stepped ledges and platforms. The upper part sits on an oblong, artificially shaped rock surrounded by some of the site’s finest ashlar. The rock's top is carved with steps and horizontal platforms and a Z-shaped edge commonly interpreted as an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Altar" title="Altar" id="mwBGY">altar</a>. The upper chamber’s wall contains embedded niches and a system of three openings (eastern, south-eastern, and northern); the eastern and south-eastern openings have stone pegs of uncertain function, and the northern opening is door-like but damaged.<sup about="#mwt636" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022174–176_159-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022174–176"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022174–176-159"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Ziółkowski"},"2":{"wt":"Kościuk"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"174–176"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022174–176-159" id="mwBGc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBGg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGk">[</span>156<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGo">]</span></span></a></sup> A trapezoidal opening known as the “Serpent’s Door” leads onto a small platform that overlooks a series of pools and affords a view of Huayna Picchu.<sup about="#mwt639" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45_157-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45-157"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"White"},"3":{"wt":"1983"},"pp":{"wt":"S37-S45"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S37–S45-157" id="mwBGs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBGw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBG0">[</span>154<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBG4">]</span></span></a></sup> Archaeoastronomical studies report that the openings create characteristic sunlight patterns and allow limited views of important <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Stellar_classification" title="Stellar classification" id="mwBG8">star groups</a> (for example the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Pleiades" title="Pleiades" id="mwBHA">Pleiades</a>);<sup about="#mwt642" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S40_160-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S40"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S40-160"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"White"},"3":{"wt":"1983"},"pp":{"wt":"S40"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornWhite1983S40-160" id="mwBHE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBHI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHM">[</span>157<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHQ">]</span></span></a></sup> however, detailed 3D analyses indicate the <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt645" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Torreón"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBHU"><i lang="es">Torreón</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt645" id="mwBHY"/> was not a highly precise astronomical instrument but rather incorporated solar orientations for ritual and ceremonial purposes.<sup about="#mwt646" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022192–193_161-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022192–193"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022192–193-161"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Ziółkowski"},"2":{"wt":"Kościuk"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"192–193"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022192–193-161" id="mwBHc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBHg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHk">[</span>158<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="24" id="mwBHs"><h4 id="Intihuatana_stone">Intihuatana stone</h4>\n<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBHw"><a href="./File:143_Intiwatana_Machu_Picchu_Peru_2406_(14977268637).jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBH0"><img 2x" alt="Stone wall with trapezoidal niches, with two carved circular stone basins on the ground in front." data-file-width="4479" data-file-height="2687" data-file-type="bitmap" height="180" width="300" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.2" id="mwBIM"/></a><figcaption id="mwBIQ">Rock-carved "mortars" in the Room of the Mortars. Once proposed as water mirrors for astronomical use, studies from 2022 have cast doubt on any calendrical function, and their original purpose remains uncertain.<sup about="#mwt649" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022203–204_162-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022203–204"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022203–204-162"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Ziółkowski"},"2":{"wt":"Kościuk"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"203–204"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022203–204-162" id="mwBIU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBIY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIc">[</span>159<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIg">]</span></span></a></sup></figcaption></figure>\n<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt652" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Intihuatana, Urubamba"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBIk"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237" about="#mwt653" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw='{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}'/></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt652" id="mwBIo">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Intihuatana,_Urubamba" title="Intihuatana, Urubamba">Intihuatana, Urubamba</a></div>\n\n<p id="mwBIs">Located on a terraced hill within the urban sector, the <i id="mwBIw">Intihuatana</i> is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ritual" title="Ritual" id="mwBI0">ritual</a> stone which the Incas used. The stone is designed to point directly at the Sun during the winter <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Solstice" title="Solstice" id="mwBI4">solstice</a>.<sup about="#mwt654" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAmao201278_163-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAmao201278"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmao201278-163"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Amao"},"2":{"wt":"2012"},"p":{"wt":"78"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmao201278-163" id="mwBI8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJE">[</span>160<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJI">]</span></span></a></sup> The name of the stone, likely attributed by Bingham due to a similar monument in Pisac, comes from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Quechuan_languages" title="Quechuan languages" id="mwBJM">Quechua</a> and means "place where the sun is tied". While its exact function is debated, scholars generally reject the popular idea that it served as a solar calendar <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Gnomon" title="Gnomon" id="mwBJQ">gnomon</a>. Instead, it may have been used for horizontal solar observations and was aligned with sacred mountains and cardinal directions.<sup about="#mwt657" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022193–195_164-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022193–195"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022193–195-164"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Ziółkowski"},"2":{"wt":"Kościuk"},"3":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"193–195"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZiółkowskiKościuk2022193–195-164" id="mwBJU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJc">[</span>161<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJg">]</span></span></a></sup> The stone is situated at 13°9'48" S. At midday on 11 November and 30 January, the Sun is situated almost exactly above the pillar, casting no shadow. On 21 June, the stone casts the longest shadow on its southern side, and on 21 December, a much shorter shadow on its northern side.<sup about="#mwt660" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDolan2021295–336_165-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDolan2021295–336"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDolan2021295–336-165"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dolan"},"2":{"wt":"2021"},"pp":{"wt":"295–336"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDolan2021295–336-165" id="mwBJk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJs">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJw">]</span></span></a></sup> Its placement may have held symbolic significance within a sacred landscape, aligning with prominent surrounding peaks such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Veronica_(mountain)" title="Veronica (mountain)" id="mwBJ0">Veronica</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Salcantay" title="Salcantay" id="mwBJ4">Salcantay</a>, and Huayna Picchu.<sup about="#mwt663" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReinhard200763–66_166-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEReinhard200763–66"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200763–66-166"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Reinhard"},"2":{"wt":"2007"},"pp":{"wt":"63–66"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200763–66-166" id="mwBJ8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBKA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKE">[</span>163<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="25" id="mwBKM"><h4 id="Inti_Mach'ay_and_the_Royal_Feast_of_the_Sun"><span id="Inti_Mach.27ay_and_the_Royal_Feast_of_the_Sun" typeof="mw:FallbackId"></span>Inti Mach'ay and the Royal Feast of the Sun</h4>\n<p id="mwBKQ">Inti Mach'ay is a special cave used to observe the Royal Feast of the Sun. This festival was celebrated during the Incan month of <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt666" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Qhapaq Raymi"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBKU"><i lang="qu">Qhapaq Raymi</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt666" id="mwBKY"/>. It began earlier in the month and concluded on the December solstice. On this day, noble boys were initiated into manhood by an ear-piercing ritual as they stood inside the cave and watched the sunrise.<sup about="#mwt667" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987346_167-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987346"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987346-167"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"Schreiber"},"3":{"wt":"White"},"4":{"wt":"1987"},"p":{"wt":"346"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987346-167" id="mwBKc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBKg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKk">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBKs">Architecturally, Inti Mach'ay is often considered to be one of the most significant structures at Machu Picchu. Its entrances, walls, steps, and windows display some of the finest masonry in the Inca Empire. The cave also includes a tunnel-like window unique among Incan structures, designed so that sunlight enters the interior only for a few days around the December solstice. This precise alignment suggests that Inti Mach'ay functioned as a solar observatory associated with the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt670" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Capac Raymi"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBKw"><i lang="qu">Capac Raymi</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt670" id="mwBK0"/> festival.<sup about="#mwt671" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349–51_168-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349–51"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349–51-168"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"Schreiber"},"3":{"wt":"White"},"4":{"wt":"1987"},"pp":{"wt":"349–51"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349–51-168" id="mwBK4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBK8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLA">[</span>165<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLE">]</span></span></a></sup> Inti Mach'ay is located on Machu Picchu's eastern side, just north of the "Condor Stone". Many of the caves surrounding this area were prehistorically used as tombs, yet there is no evidence that Mach'ay was a burial ground.<sup about="#mwt674" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349_169-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349-169"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Dearborn"},"2":{"wt":"Schreiber"},"3":{"wt":"White"},"4":{"wt":"1987"},"p":{"wt":"349"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDearbornSchreiberWhite1987349-169" id="mwBLI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBLM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLQ">[</span>166<span about="#mwt685" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAstete201235–37_171-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" Four terraces at the base of the wall retain the platform on its exterior face.<sup about="#mwt688" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67_153-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a67-153"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Millones"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"p":{"wt":"67"}},"i":0}}]}'><a id="mwBM4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBM8">From within the temple, one can observe both sunrise and sunset across the ruins and surrounding mountains.<sup about="#mwt691" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a74_172-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMillones2020a74-172" id="mwBNA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBNE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNI">[</span>169<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNM">]</span></span></a></sup> Evidence suggests it was originally roofed by a three‑wall timber truss system resting on wooden beams and pilasters set into side pockets in the masonry.<sup about="#mwt694" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a430–431_173-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a430–431"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a430–431-173"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Puelles"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"430–431"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a430–431-173" id="mwBNQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBNU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNY">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBNg">During his 1911 visit, Hiram Bingham recorded a charcoal inscription on the central window reading "Lizárraga 1902", left by Agustín Lizárraga. The graffiti appears in Bingham's early photographs, published in <i id="mwBNk"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./The_Geographical_Journal" title="The Geographical Journal" id="mwBNo">The Geographical Magazine</a></i> (April 1912), indicating prior local knowledge and clearing of the site.<sup about="#mwt697" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBastante2020a31_174-0" rel="dc:references" id="mwBOA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="27" id="mwBOE"><h3 id="Construction">Construction</h3>\n<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt700" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Incan architecture"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBOI"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1368532237" about="#mwt701" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Incan_architecture" title="Incan architecture" class="mw-redirect">Incan architecture</a></div>\n\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBOY"/></a><figcaption id="mwBOc">Residential section with closely joined stones typical of Inca dry masonry</figcaption></figure>\n\n<p id="mwBOg">The central buildings of Machu Picchu are built in classical Inca <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ashlar_masonry" title="Ashlar masonry" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBOk">dry masonry</a>, with large blocks precisely shaped through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Quarrying" title="Quarrying" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBOo">quarrying</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Stone-cutting" title="Stone-cutting" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBOs">stone-cutting</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Stone-dressing" title="Stone-dressing" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBOw">stone-dressing</a>, then fitted together without <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Mortar_(masonry)" title="Mortar (masonry)" id="mwBO0">mortar</a>.<sup about="#mwt702" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMasiniAbateScavoneLasaponara2022151–161_175-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMasiniAbateScavoneLasaponara2022151–161"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMasiniAbateScavoneLasaponara2022151–161-175"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Masini"},"2":{"wt":"Abate"},"3":{"wt":"Scavone"},"4":{"wt":"Lasaponara"},"5":{"wt":"2022"},"pp":{"wt":"151–161"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMasiniAbateScavoneLasaponara2022151–161-175" id="mwBO4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBO8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPA">[</span>172<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPE">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBPI">The site may have been intentionally built on fault lines to provide natural drainage and a source of fractured stone for construction. According to geologist Rualdo Menegat, Machu Picchu "shows us that the Incan civilization was an empire of fractured rocks."<sup about="#mwt710" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-176" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-176"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-176" id="mwBPM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBPQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPU">[</span>173<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt705" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMenegat20191_177-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMenegat20191"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMenegat20191-177"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Menegat"},"2":{"wt":"2019"},"p":{"wt":"1"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMenegat20191-177" id="mwBPc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBPg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPk">[</span>174<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBPs"><a href="./File:Peru-190_(2217899833).jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBPw"><img resource="./File:Peru-190_(2217899833).jpg" 2x" alt="Panoramic view of an Inca quarry with terraces and a pile of large, irregular granite blocks." data-file-width="6816" data-file-height="4432" data-file-type="bitmap" height="163" width="250" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBP0"/></a><figcaption id="mwBP4">Inca quarry at Machu Picchu, where large irregular granite blocks from a natural <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Blockfield" title="Blockfield" id="mwBP8">granitic chaos</a> were used as building stone.</figcaption></figure>\n<p id="mwBQA">The section of the mountain where Machu Picchu was built provided various challenges that the Incas solved with local materials. One issue was the seismic activity due to two fault lines, which made mortar and similar building methods nearly useless. Instead, the Inca mined stones from some quarries at the site,<sup about="#mwt711" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETripcevichVaughn201252_178-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTETripcevichVaughn201252"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTETripcevichVaughn201252-178"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Tripcevich"},"2":{"wt":"Vaughn"},"3":{"wt":"2012"},"p":{"wt":"52"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTETripcevichVaughn201252-178" id="mwBQE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQM">[</span>175<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQQ">]</span></span></a></sup> including one identified in 2023 using remote sensing techniques, which was probably located in the catchment area between the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Government_of_the_Inca_Empire#Hurin_Suyukuna,_or_the_Lower_Quarters" title="Government of the Inca Empire" id="mwBQU">Hurin</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Government_of_the_Inca_Empire#Hanan_Suyukuna,_or_the_Upper_Quarters" title="Government of the Inca Empire" id="mwBQY">Hanan</a> before it was covered over to create the current <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt714" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Plaza Principal"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBQc"><i lang="es">Plaza Principal</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt714" id="mwBQg"/>.<sup about="#mwt715" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMasiniRomanoSieczkowska202316035_179-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMasiniRomanoSieczkowska202316035"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMasiniRomanoSieczkowska202316035-179"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Masini"},"2":{"wt":"Romano"},"3":{"wt":"Sieczkowska"},"4":{"wt":"2023"},"p":{"wt":"16035"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMasiniRomanoSieczkowska202316035-179" id="mwBQk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQs">[</span>176<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQw">]</span></span></a></sup> Once mined, the Inca lined the granite stones up and shaped them to fit together perfectly, stabilizing the structures. Inca walls have many stabilizing features: doors and windows are trapezoidal, narrowing from bottom to top; corners are usually rounded; inside corners often incline slightly into the rooms, and L-shaped blocks are often tied together outside corners; walls are offset slightly from row to row rather than rising straight from bottom to top.<sup about="#mwt718" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAstete2020a313–326_180-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEAstete2020a313–326"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstete2020a313–326-180"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Astete"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"313–326"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstete2020a313–326-180" id="mwBQ0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQ4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQ8">[</span>177<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBRE">Heavy rainfall required terraces to drain rainwater and prevent mudslides, landslides, erosion, and flooding. Terraces were layered with stone chips, sand, dirt, and topsoil to absorb water and prevent it from running down the mountain. Similar layering protected the large city center from flooding.<sup about="#mwt721" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra2000_181-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEWrightValencia Zegarra2000"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra2000-181"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Wright"},"2":{"wt":"Valencia Zegarra"},"3":{"wt":"2000"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWrightValencia_Zegarra2000-181" id="mwBRI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBRM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRQ">[</span>178<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRU">]</span></span></a></sup> Multiple canals and reserves throughout the city provided water that could be supplied to the terraces for irrigation and to prevent erosion and flooding.<sup about="#mwt724" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92_48-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92-48"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Reinhard"},"2":{"wt":"2007"},"pp":{"wt":"87–92"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEReinhard200787–92-48" id="mwBRY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBRc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRg">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBRo">The approach to moving and placing the enormous stones remains uncertain, probably involving hundreds of men to push the stones up inclines. A few stones have knobs that could have been used to lever them into position; the knobs were generally sanded away, with a few overlooked. For larger stones, the Incas likely employed ramps with gentle inclines, along with wooden rollers, levers, and ropes made from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Furcraea_andina" title="Furcraea andina" id="mwBRs">maguey</a> fibers. Most stones were moved from higher to lower elevations, but some, like those at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ollantaytambo" title="Ollantaytambo" id="mwBRw">Ollantaytambo</a>, were transported over long distances.<sup about="#mwt727" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a417–418_182-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a417–418"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a417–418-182"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Puelles"},"2":{"wt":"2020a"},"pp":{"wt":"417–418"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPuelles2020a417–418-182" id="mwBR0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBR4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBR8">[</span>179<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBSA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section><section data-mw-section-id="28" id="mwBSE"><h3 id="Transportation">Transportation</h3>\n<p id="mwBSI">Machu Picchu was connected to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_road_system" title="Inca road system" id="mwBSM">Inca road system</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Long-distance_trade" title="Long-distance trade" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBSQ">long-distance trade</a>, as shown by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Obsidian" title="Obsidian" id="mwBSU">obsidian</a> nodules found near the site’s entrance. Analyses by Burger and Asaro in the 1970s traced them to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Titicaca" title="Titicaca" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBSY">Titicaca</a> or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Chivay_obsidian_source" title="Chivay obsidian source" id="mwBSc">Chivay sources</a>, indicating extensive <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Pre-Hispanic" title="Pre-Hispanic" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBSg">pre-Hispanic</a> exchange networks.<sup about="#mwt730" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200497_183-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200497"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200497-183"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Burger"},"2":{"wt":"Salazar"},"3":{"wt":"2004"},"p":{"wt":"97"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurgerSalazar200497-183" id="mwBSk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBSo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBSs">[</span>180<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBSw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBS0"><a Trail</a>, one of the site's three principal access routes</figcaption></figure>\n\n<p id="mwBTI">Today, visitors can reach Machu Picchu via three main routes. The most popular option is the train journey from Cusco or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Ollantaytambo" title="Ollantaytambo" id="mwBTM">Ollantaytambo</a>. Operated by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./PeruRail" title="PeruRail" id="mwBTQ">PeruRail</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_Rail" title="Inca Rail" id="mwBTU">Inca Rail</a>, this route takes visitors to the town of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Aguas_Calientes,_Peru" title="Aguas Calientes, Peru" id="mwBTY">Aguas Calientes</a>, from where they can take a bus ride of <span about="#mwt733" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"8.6"},"2":{"wt":"km"},"3":{"wt":"mi"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBTc">8.6 kilometres (5.3</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt733"> </span><span about="#mwt733">mi)</span> or walk to the Machu Picchu entrance.<sup about="#mwt734" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201594_184-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201594"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201594-184"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"SERNANP"},"2":{"wt":"DCC"},"3":{"wt":"2015"},"p":{"wt":"94"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201594-184" id="mwBTg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBTk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTo">[</span>181<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTs">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBTw">Another widely chosen route is the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Inca_Trail_to_Machu_Picchu" title="Inca Trail to Machu Picchu" id="mwBT0">Inca Trail</a>, a historic path built by the Incas considered "the most famous hike in South America" by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Lonely_Planet" title="Lonely Planet" id="mwBT4">Lonely Planet</a>,<sup about="#mwt737" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESainsburyEgertonJohansonMcCarthy2021_185-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESainsburyEgertonJohansonMcCarthy2021"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESainsburyEgertonJohansonMcCarthy2021-185"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Sainsbury"},"2":{"wt":"Egerton"},"3":{"wt":"Johanson"},"4":{"wt":"McCarthy"},"5":{"wt":"2021"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESainsburyEgertonJohansonMcCarthy2021-185" id="mwBT8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBUA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUE">[</span>182<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUI">]</span></span></a></sup> attracting thousands of tourists each year.<sup about="#mwt740" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._62-64_186-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table No. 62-64"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._62-64-186"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"MINCETUR"},"2":{"wt":"2026"},"loc":{"wt":"Table No. 62-64"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMINCETUR2026Table_No._62-64-186" id="mwBUM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBUQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUU">[</span>183<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUY">]</span></span></a></sup>\nThe trail begins at either <span title="Spanish-language text" about="#mwt743" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"es"},"2":{"wt":"Piscacucho"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBUc"><i lang="es">Piscacucho</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Spanish-language_text" about="#mwt743" id="mwBUg"/> (Km 82 on the railway to Aguas Calientes) or <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt744" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Q&apos;oriwayrachina"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBUk"><i lang="qu">Q'oriwayrachina</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt744" id="mwBUo"/> (Km 104), and, depending on the starting point, spans up to approximately <span about="#mwt745" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"42.5"},"2":{"wt":"km"},"3":{"wt":"mi"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBUs">42.5 kilometres (26.4</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt745"> </span><span about="#mwt745">mi)</span>, reaching an altitude of <span about="#mwt746" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"4200"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"ft"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBUw">4,200 metres (13,800</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt746"> </span><span about="#mwt746">ft)</span> at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Warmi_Wañusqa" title="Warmi Wañusqa" id="mwBU0">Warmi Wañusqa</a>. It passes through the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Andes" title="Andes" id="mwBU4">Andes</a> and various archaeological sites before reaching the <span title="Quechua-language text" about="#mwt747" typeof="mw:Transclusion" data-mw='{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"qu"},"2":{"wt":"Inti Punku"}},"i":0}}]}' id="mwBU8"><i lang="qu">Inti Punku</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Quechua-language_text" about="#mwt747" id="mwBVA"/> at Machu Picchu. Due to limited permits, booking through a tourism agency is required.<sup about="#mwt748" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHuamán_et_al.2020109–115_187-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTEHuamán et al.2020109–115"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuamán_et_al.2020109–115-187"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Huamán et al."},"2":{"wt":"2020"},"pp":{"wt":"109–115"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHuamán_et_al.2020109–115-187" id="mwBVE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBVI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVM">[</span>184<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVQ">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt753" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-188" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-188"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-188" id="mwBVU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBVY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVc">[</span>185<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBVk">Alternatively, travelers can take a less conventional route that involves traveling by road to a point near the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Hydroelectric_Station_(train_station)" title="Hydroelectric Station (train station)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBVo">Hydroelectric station</a>. From there, they can either walk or take a short train ride to Aguas Calientes.<sup about="#mwt754" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201586_189-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Transclusion mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{"group":"","name":"FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201586"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201586-189"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"sfn","href":"./Template:Sfn"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"SERNANP"},"2":{"wt":"DCC"},"3":{"wt":"2015"},"p":{"wt":"86"}},"i":0}}]}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-FOOTNOTESERNANPDCC201586-189" id="mwBVs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBVw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBV0">[</span>186<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBV4">]</span></span></a></sup> This option is generally more affordable and does not require booking, but it is less recommended during the rainy season due to potential landslide risks.<sup about="#mwt759" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-190" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-190"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-190" id="mwBV8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBWA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWE">[</span>187<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n<p id="mwBWM">As of November 2024, the construction of a new paved roadway right to the doorstep of the historic site is in progress and due for completion in 2025. The path, otherwise known as the Santa María-Santa Teresa-Machu Picchu Hydroelectric Bridge highway, involves 28.41 kilometers (22 miles) of asphalt-paved roads that would generally reduce access time to the heritage site from 4 or 5 hours to 2 hours.<sup about="#mwt762" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-191" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw='{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-191"}}'><a href="./Machu_Picchu#cite_note-191" id="mwBWQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBWU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWY">[</span>188<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>\n\n</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="29" id="mwBWg"><h2 id="In_popular_culture">In popular culture</h2>\n<p id="mwBWk">Machu Picchu has appeared in several films, television programmes and music productions. The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Paramount_Pictures" title="Paramount Pictures" id="mwBWo">Paramount Pictures</a> film <i id="mwBWs"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Secret_of_the_Incas" title="Secret of the Incas" id="mwBWw">Secret of the Incas</a></i> (1954), starring <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Charlton_Heston" title="Charlton Heston" id="mwBW0">Charlton Heston</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="./Yma_Sumac" title="Yma Sumac" id="mwBW4">Yma Sumac</a>, was filmed on location at Machu Picchu and Cusco, marking the first time a major Hollywood studio shot on site.<sup about="#mwt772" in the Machu Picchu area and on the stone stairway of Huayna Picchu.<sup about="#mwt763" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHerzogCronin2002_193-0" rel="dc:references"
